newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CHEAPER FOOD COMES TO RESCUE OF S.AFRICA INFLATION.
newsitem.headline: CHEAPER FOOD COMES TO RESCUE OF S.AFRICA INFLATION.

text.p: Volatile food prices came to the rescue of South African inflation in November with an unchanged monthly food component giving a better-than-expected result, fuelling hopes CPI will be capped below 10 percent.

Economists, who had been predicting a 9.5 percent year-on-year increase in the consumer price index (CPI) on the back of higher food costs, said they were surprised by the data, but added it augured well for the December figure.
CPI rose only 9.2 percent in November, little changed from October's 9.1 percent, while the month-on-month rate of increase was 0.4 percent versus 1.0.

The Central Statistical Service said a flat food price index in November reflected higher prices for grain, meat, fish and dairy products, offset by falls in the cost of vegetables, sugar, coffee and tea.
The two main contributors to the modest 0.4 percent increase in non-food items were housing and transport costs.
The latest rise in headline inflation was the seventh in succession and takes the CPI to a 17-month high. But economists believe South African inflation is now nearing its peak.

"We still look for an increase in December but with November coming in quite a bit below forecast we can be more optimistic that CPI can be contained below the 10 percent level," said Julia Roy, treasury economist at Rand Merchant Bank.
Roy said the flat food price picture in November gave grounds to hope that South Africa was finally seeing the unwinding of the very high food price increases of recent months.
Nedcor economist Magan Mistry agreed it looked as if CPI would peak below 10 percent in December, despite the impact of higher fuel prices and higher mortgage costs this month.
Mistry said he saw price rises starting to tail off in the new year under the influence of flagging consumer demand, following November's one point rate hike.
"I think December will be the peak because demand will start weakening in January and February," he said.
"It also looks like we should have another good agricultural season which should benefit prices."

For 1996 as a whole, economists expect inflation to average around 7.5 percent, down from 8.7 percent in 1995. But the average rate will inevitably pick up in 1997 as inflation plateaus at a relatively high level, reflecting the impact of the rand's fall this year.

South Africa's consumer inflation rate sank to a 24-year low of 5.5 percent in April but has been climbing since in reaction to the sharp fall in the rand which has lost around 30 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since February.

The good November inflation figures gave a fillip to government bonds with the yield of the benchmark R150 issue falling 10 basis points after the news to stand around 16.16 percent, down from 16.195 on Wednesday.
